newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela to use kid gloves to reduce bureaucracy.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to use kid gloves to reduce bureaucracy.

text.p: Venezuela will use kid gloves rather than an ax to reduce its huge state bureaucracy, Venezuelan Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said on Monday.
Petkoff acknowledged in an interview that Venezuela's central administration has an army of about 800,000 employees, more public servants than richer and more populous Japan.

"To unravel the hypertrophiated monster that the Venezuelan state has turned into will require a lot of political will as well as kid gloves," Petkoff told Reuters. "No one's talking of taking an ax to it".

The former guerrilla leader, who is attending the joint annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, blamed massive state employment on the legacy of 35 years of populism in Venezuela.
President Rafael Caldera, faced with a crumbling economy, earlier this year decided to cut ties with the past and sought the IMF's support to overhaul his country's public sector.
However, to bring state employment down to manageable proportions, he will have to deal with deeply entrenched political, social and even personal interests, Petkoff said.
To make things worse, Caldera's administration lacks a majority in Venezuela's Congress, which will have to approve labor reforms.
The plain-spoken Petkoff said little had changed since the IMF, the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank pledged to help Venezuela in April.
But on the upside, the country's main political parties now all agree that the public sector must be shrunk.
According to Petkoff, eight of Venezuela's 16 ministries have completed proposals to reduce their payrolls, including the mammoth education ministry, with some 200,000 employees.
Adding insult to injury,the quality of Venezuelan education is dismal.
Highlighting the political sensitivity of the issue, Petkoff refused to put a number on the ideal size for the public bureaucracy.
"There are no preconceived number. It's neither possible nor convenient to set goals or percentages of decreases, because we would only generate resistance," he argued.
Petkoff complained about one recent front page story in a Caracas newspaper that predicted that 500,000 people would lose their state jobs, calling such forecasts irresponsible.
Despite the uncertainty, Caldera's administration has managed to bring labor leaders on board, at least nominally.
But Petkoff knows that unions will tend to defend their natural interests when it comes down to the wire.
"Practice is not always what is preached, and this is where we will need kid gloves," he said.
In order to induce voluntary retirement, the government streamlined the severance payment system. People who decide to quit will get paid in two months, rather than 18 months.
Another glitch to overcome is what is know in Venezuela as "pre-retirement", a system under which people who reach retirement age are simply sent home but stay on the payroll.
"This is something we will have to push during the two years left in this administration in order to reach a point of no return," he said.
